🧒 In plain words first

The tools from the last few stops (slopes, the chain rule, chances, tables of numbers) are used here to explain the most important formulas in real models. It is like learning to add and multiply, then doing some real sums.

Each one is proved step by step, with its assumptions spelled out. Once you follow them, you see why models are built the way they are: not by guesswork, but so that the “how to adjust” message reaches every knob.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

The first four stops built the tools; here they are applied to the real model: Backprop derivation, the output layer’s Softmax + CE gradient p − y, attention’s Attention’s √dₖ scaling, Gradient through residuals, and the Policy gradient used in post-training. Each is proved step by step with its assumptions stated.

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

A network is an assembly line, one layer after another. Once you know how wrong the final answer is, you need to know which way, and how far, to turn every knob.

Backpropagation is like passing a message back from the finish line: the last layer works out “how much of the error is my fault”, then shares that blame with the layer before it according to how thick each connection is (the weights), and so on back, layer by layer. Each layer reuses what the layer after it already worked out, so going backwards costs about as much as going forwards once, instead of a separate calculation for every knob.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

To be more exact…The “blame” is, precisely, the partial derivative of the loss with respect to each layer’s in-between result (called the “error signal”). “About as much work” means the same order of magnitude (within a constant factor), not exactly equal.

The network: input xxx, an activation φ\varphiφ applied element-wise, loss L=ℓ(z(2))L=\ell(z^{(2)})L=ℓ(z(2)).

🔤 What the symbols mean

  • Say: “z”the in-between result after the weighted sum (before the activation function)
  • Say: “layer …” (the raised label in brackets)a raised number or letter in brackets says “which layer”; it is not a power
  • Say: “W”the weights: a table of numbers saying how thick each connection is
  • Say: no word: side by side means timesTwo things written right next to each other, with no sign between them, are multiplied: a number right before a letter means that number times it; two brackets side by side are multiplied.

  • Say: “b”the bias: one extra number added to each output
  • Say: “h”the in-between result after the activation function (the hidden layer)
  • Say: “phi”the activation function: bends each number on its own
  • Say: “… of …”What comes out when you put the thing in brackets into the “machine” (function) named in front. Like a vending machine: put something in, get something out.

Q.E.D. ∎

The key is that δ(l)\delta^{(l)}δ(l) comes from δ(l+1)\delta^{(l+1)}δ(l+1) by one matrix product, reusing the later layer’s work, so one backward pass costs the same order as one forward pass instead of one pass per parameter. This is the algorithm Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams published in Nature in 1986.

⚠️ Mix-up

🧒 In plain words first

Backpropagation is measuring the slope: trace back from the result to work out which way, and how much, each knob should turn. Gradient descent is actually turning them a little by those numbers. Measure first, then turn.

In one line: backpropagation computes the gradient: with the chain rule it works backwards from the loss, layer by layer, to every parameter’s partial derivative; gradient descent uses it: parameter − learning rate × gradient. One “measures the slope”, the other “takes the step”.

CompareBackpropagationGradient descent (and optimizers like Adam)
Doescomputes gradientsupdates parameters with them
Relies onthe chain rule, back to frontan update rule: θ ← θ − η·g
Changes parameters?no, it only produces numbersyes
Swappable?stays the same when you change optimizerSGD, momentum and Adam are different versions of this step
  1. Forward: feed a batch through the layers to the output and get the loss.
  2. Backpropagation: work back from the loss to get every parameter’s gradient.
  3. Update: the optimizer (gradient descent, Adam, …) changes the parameters using the gradients. These three together make one training step.

🧠 Remember: backpropagation computes, never changes; gradient descent takes the result and changes.

🧒 In plain words first

The smallest network: w₁ and w₂ are two knobs (weights), x is the input, y the correct answer, h the in-between result, ŷ (y with a hat) the model’s output, L the loss, and σ a function that squeezes numbers to between 0 and 1. Drag w₁ and w₂ and compare the two columns: one works out the slope with the derived formula, the other by brute force: “nudge the knob a tiny bit and see how much the loss changes”.

ⓘ A minimal network: h = σ(w₁x), ŷ = w₂h, L = ½(ŷ − y)², with x = 1 and y = 1 fixed (illustrative); both methods are computed exactly.

Why it’s built this way:
  • A derivation can be checked numerically: both methods should give almost the same gradient. Framework developers test this way too.
👀 Try this:
  • Set any w₁, w₂: the two columns agree to about 7 decimal places (relative error around 10⁻⁸ or less).
  • Watch the σ′ = h(1 − h) row: 0.25 at w₁ = 0, only about 0.045 at ±3. Every gradient reaching w₁ is multiplied by this factor; that is how saturation shrinks gradients.
③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

The model scores every word, softmax turns the scores into chances, and cross-entropy scores “how badly it guessed”. The result is strikingly simple: how to adjust each score is just “the model’s chance − the correct answer’s chance”.

For example (illustrative), if the model gives the correct word only a 0.3 chance: 0.3 − 1 = −0.7, a negative slope, so walking downhill raises that word’s score; a wrong word given 0.2: 0.2 − 0 = 0.2, so its score is lowered. The worse the mistake, the bigger the adjustment; as long as the guess is not right yet, this difference does not shrink to 0 just because the scores are extreme.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

To be more exact…“The correct answer’s chance” can be a table with a single 1 and 0 everywhere else (one-hot), or any distribution that adds up to 1; the result holds either way. Every difference lies between −1 and 1.

Output scores zzz, p=softmax⁡(z)p=\operatorname{softmax}(z)p=softmax(z), target distribution yyy (yk≥0, ∑kyk=1y_k\ge0,\ \sum_k y_k=1yk​≥0, ∑k​yk​=1; one-hot is a special case), loss L=−∑kyklog⁡pkL=-\sum_k y_k\log p_kL=−∑k​yk​logpk​.

🔤 Symbols in this card’s text

  • Say: “softmax”Turns a list of scores into chances: each between 0 and 1, all adding up to 1, higher score, bigger chance.
  • Say: “greater than or equal to”The left side is bigger, or the same. “≥ 0” means “not negative”.
  • Say: “divided by” (slash)Another way to write division: 6/3 means 6÷3 = 2.

Explained above:

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

In attention, each word takes its own list of numbers (the query) and multiplies it position by position with another word’s list (the key), adding everything up into a match score. The longer the lists, the more terms get added, and the more easily the score becomes very large or very small, just as the total from tossing 64 coins (heads +1, tails −1) swings far more than a single toss.

When scores are too far apart, softmax hands nearly all the chance to one word, and the others hardly learn anything. So the score is first divided by the square root of the length, bringing the swings back to normal size.

🧒 In plain words first

A residual connection: each layer does not replace its input outright; it adds a small change on top: output = input + change. Like marking up a draft essay instead of rewriting it from scratch every time.

The payoff comes when the message travels back: there is always a direct road on which the message goes from the last layer back to the first unchanged. Without it, every layer can shrink the message; if (illustrative) each layer halves it, after 20 layers almost nothing is left.

🧒 In plain words first

When training a model on problems, sometimes all you know is “1 point if right, 0 if wrong”, not “how far off”. A score like that has no slope on its own.

The trick: let the model answer many times; for answers that did well, raise the chance of each of their words a little; for answers that did badly, lower it. Smarter still is to compare with the average score: raise only what beats the average and lower what falls below it, which makes learning steadier.

To be more exact…Precisely, what gets optimised is “the score you get on average” (the expected reward), which can be differentiated with respect to the knobs. Subtracting the average (a baseline) leaves the gradient’s expected value unchanged and only reduces its wobble (variance); the baseline may depend on the problem, but not on this particular answer.

    Why: An answer’s probability is the product of word-by-word conditionals (Probability stop); the log turns it into a sum.

So (R(y)−b) ∇θlog⁡πθ(y∣x)(R(y)-b)\,\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y\mid x)(R(y)−b)∇θ​logπθ​(y∣x) is an unbiased estimate, and a bbb near the average reward (for instance the mean score of several samples for the same prompt) cuts the variance a lot. Intuitively: raise the probability of every word in answers better than average, lower it for worse ones.
